chapter.title: Enzymes
chapter.scopeNote: Original condensed MCAT biochemistry lessons covering the declared outline sections. This release is implemented, not independently scientifically verified; it is not exhaustive textbook coverage.

steps.text: Enzymes accelerate reactions by lowering the activation free-energy barrier. They are regenerated during a catalytic cycle rather than consumed stoichiometrically.
A catalyst does not change the free-energy difference between reactants and products, the equilibrium constant, or the equilibrium composition at fixed conditions.
Both forward and reverse reactions can accelerate. An enzyme cannot make an isolated thermodynamically unfavorable conversion favorable merely by binding substrate.
Coupling to a favorable reaction can drive a net process. Separate this change in the overall reaction from catalysis of an unchanged reaction.

steps.text: Active sites bring reactants into useful orientations and provide a local chemical environment. Induced fit means binding and conformation influence one another.
General acid/base catalysis transfers protons. Covalent catalysis temporarily links enzyme and substrate; metal ions may stabilize charge or organize reacting groups.
Preferential stabilization of a transition state lowers the barrier. Binding the ground-state substrate extremely tightly without transition-state stabilization can impede turnover.
Organic coenzymes and inorganic cofactors can participate in catalysis. A missing required cofactor can limit activity even when the protein sequence is normal.

steps.text: For a simple Michaelis–Menten enzyme measured at initial rate, v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]). At [S] = Km, v equals half of Vmax.
At saturating substrate, v approaches Vmax. With all else fixed, increasing active enzyme concentration increases Vmax; kcat is Vmax divided by total active enzyme concentration.
Ideal competitive inhibition increases apparent Km without changing Vmax. Pure noncompetitive inhibition decreases Vmax without changing Km; mixed inhibition need not preserve Km.
Cooperative enzymes may show sigmoidal rather than Michaelis–Menten behavior. Km is not universally a direct dissociation constant or a universal measure of affinity.

lessons.title: Effects of Local Conditions on Enzyme Activity

steps.text: Temperature affects collision rates and conformational stability. Warming can increase rate over one range but reduce activity when unfolding becomes important.
pH changes the protonation of catalytic and binding groups. A suitable pH for one enzyme is not a universal optimum for all enzymes.
A pH-dependent activity change can occur without global unfolding. Distinguish altered active-site ionization from irreversible structural damage.
To compare conditions, hold substrate, enzyme amount and assay time constant. A measured endpoint after prolonged incubation is not automatically an initial rate.

steps.text: Allosteric regulators bind at sites distinct from the active site and alter function through conformational effects. Allosteric regulation can activate or inhibit.
Reversible phosphorylation changes some enzymes’ activities; its effect depends on the particular enzyme. Phosphorylation is not a universal on switch.
An end product can inhibit an earlier pathway step, limiting excess production. This feedback mechanism is distinct from merely exhausting the initial substrate.
Proteolytic activation of a zymogen is often effectively irreversible. Changes in transcription or degradation change enzyme abundance on a different timescale.
